title: The Labor Demand Curve is Downward Sloping: Reexamining the Impact of Immigration on the Labor Market
research_question: How does an influx of immigrant workers affect the wages and employment outcomes of native workers who compete with them in the labor market? Specifically, to what extent do increases in labor supply within narrowly defined skill groups (defined by both schooling and work experience) reduce the wages and labor supply of similarly skilled native workers in the United States?
data_description: The analysis uses microdata from the 1960, 1970, 1980, and 1990 Public Use Microdata Samples of the U.S. Decennial Census, combined with the pooled 1999, 2000, and 2001 Annual Demographic Supplements of the Current Population Survey (treated as a 2000 cross section). The sample is restricted to men aged 18–64 in the civilian labor force, with immigrants identified as foreign-born noncitizens or naturalized citizens. Workers are classified into four education categories (high school dropouts, high school graduates, some college, college graduates) and eight five-year experience cells (1–40 years), with experience computed as age minus assumed age of labor market entry. Key variables include log annual earnings, log weekly earnings (deflated to 1999 dollars via CPI-U), fraction of time worked, and the immigrant share of each education-experience cell. Earnings are measured for wage and salary workers with positive earnings who are not enrolled in school.
institutional_context: The United States experienced a major resurgence of large-scale immigration following the 1965 Amendments to the Immigration and Nationality Act, with the foreign-born share of the male labor force rising substantially between 1960 and 2000. Immigrants are heavily concentrated geographically — in 1990, about a third lived in just three metropolitan areas (Los Angeles, New York, Miami) — and the skill composition of arrivals shifted notably toward less-educated workers in the 1980s and 1990s. Importantly, the immigrant supply shock was unevenly distributed not only across schooling categories but also across experience levels within schooling categories, and these imbalances changed across decades. For instance, immigration disproportionately raised the supply of high school dropouts with mid-range experience by 2000, while the pattern was very different in 1960. This setting motivates examining how immigrant inflows alter the labor market opportunities of competing native workers defined by both education and experience.
